headline: The Bar East of the Jetty Moved Again — And the Bass Found the New Cut
subhead: Junky ocean swell pushed bait and stripers into the throat of Moriches Inlet this week, with the real bite happening where the shifted sandbar meets the channel edge.
body_markdown:
I walked the east side of the inlet jetty at Cupsogue on Wednesday's low and the bottom read different than it did two weeks ago. The bar that usually sits tight against the rocks has slid east another fifteen, maybe twenty yards, and it's built up a shoulder where there used to be a smooth taper into the channel. That's not unusual for August — this inlet never sits still, it's been rebuilding itself since the '92 nor'easter reshaped the whole throat, and every blow since keeps nudging sand around the jetty tips. What matters for you is that the new shoulder creates a sharper drop-off, maybe six feet of relief in twenty yards, right where the ebb current funnels hardest. That's exactly the kind of edge stripers hold on, and this week they did.

The ocean's been running short and junky — the swell off the Bight has been sitting around four feet at five seconds, which is a mess for surfcasting the open beach but it's actually good news inside. That kind of chop keeps bait pushed off the outer bars and funneling into the inlet mouth, and the fish follow it. Cupsogue regulars who fished the last two hours of the ebb into dead low found bass holding right on that new drop, taking 1.5-ounce bucktails cast up-current and swung down across the seam, worked with a slow lift-and-drop on the bottom third of the retrieve. Nothing oversized — mostly 24 to 30 inches, a mix of school fish and a few solid slot bass — but consistent enough that guys were putting three or four in the box before the tide went dead. Same pattern held on the inside edge of the west jetty on the front of the flood, though that bite's shorter-lived, maybe 90 minutes before the current gets too soft to hold fish tight to structure.

Don't bother with the middle of the day right now. Bay water's been sitting warm through the afternoon — enough that the bite compresses hard into the first two hours of light and the last two before dark. I fished a noon tide Tuesday off Tuthill Point and never had a sniff; came back at 6 p.m. on the same tide stage two days later and it was a different bay. That's the pattern to plan around for the next week or two — mornings and evenings, skip the heat of the day unless you're specifically working deep holes.

Bluefish are the one thing that's been reliable no matter what the tide chart says. Snapper blues are thick in the back creeks off East Moriches and around the Forge River mouth — small, aggressive, and a great way to keep a kid busy on light spinning gear and a piece of spearing. We flagged this a couple weeks back, that the snapper class would build into real adult fish by late August, and that's exactly what's showing now. Out at the inlet itself, adult blues in the 3-5 pound range are mixing into the same current seams as the bass, and they'll hit the same bucktails, though a wire leader saves you some heartache. Topwater poppers thrown into visible boils off the jetty rocks on the last of the ebb have been drawing violent strikes — that bite doesn't last long once the current slacks, so you have to be ready when the boils show.

Fluke fishing inside the bay has been unremarkable — a lot of shorts, a scattered few keepers — and that tracks with what's happening in warmer, stagnant bay water across the whole South Shore this time of year. The better fish are holding tighter to the inlet channel itself, where tidal exchange keeps water a few degrees cooler than the flats up toward Mastic. Working the edges of the marked channel with a 3/4-ounce white bucktail and a Gulp swimming mullet, dragged slow along the bottom on the last of the incoming, has been the most consistent way to find a keeper in that 19-inch range. It's not a numbers game right now — plan on covering water.

Weakfish remain thin. I'm not going to pretend otherwise — the stock's been down for years and this August is no different. If you pick one up drifting a bucktail tipped with squid strip along the deeper holes off Pattersquash in low light, treat it as a bonus, not a target species. Porgies, on the other hand, have been steady and dependable on the bay bottom off Tuthill Point and around the East Moriches flats — sandworms or clam on a simple hi-lo rig, 15 to 20 feet of water, good action for a slower afternoon when the bigger stuff isn't cooperating. Blackfish season's still weeks off, so leave the tautog gear in the garage for now.

Looking ahead, the tides are building back toward the August 28 full moon, which should sharpen up that current edge at the new bar shoulder even more — stronger flow means a tighter, more defined seam for the bass to sit on. If the ocean swell backs off some, I'd also expect the surf bite at Cupsogue proper to pick back up, since calmer water lets fish work closer to the beach instead of holding deep in the inlet throat. Until then, work the tide stages tight, fish the edges the storms and swells keep redrawing, and don't waste daylight hours you don't have to.
